lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text_puhe: Moi! Keittiön tiskialtaan alla on vettä.
lines.text_kirja: Hei! Keittiön tiskialtaan alla on vettä.
lines.gloss_en: Hi! There's water under the kitchen sink.

judge.reason: Moi and hei are both greetings; the rest is identical.

puhe.text: Moi! Keittiön tiskialtaan alla on vettä.

kirja.text: Hei! Keittiön tiskialtaan alla on vettä.

lines.speaker: Raimo
lines.gloss_en: Oh no. How much is there?

judge.reason: Paljonks is the spoken form of paljonko; same question.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: A small puddle. It's dripping from the pipe.

judge.reason: Putkest is the spoken form of putkesta; same meaning.

lines.speaker: Raimo
lines.text_puhe: Laita ämpäri alle. Mä tuun tunnin päästä.
lines.text_kirja: Laita ämpäri alle. Minä tulen tunnin päästä.
lines.gloss_en: Put a bucket under it. I'll come in an hour.

judge.reason: Mä tuun is the spoken form of minä tulen; both say 'in an hour'.

puhe.text: Laita ämpäri alle. Mä tuun tunnin päästä.

kirja.text: Laita ämpäri alle. Minä tulen tunnin päästä.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: Thanks. Should I turn off the water?

judge.reason: Kiitti/kiitos and pitääks mun/pitääkö minun are register differences only.

lines.speaker: Raimo
lines.text_puhe: Ei tarvii, jos se tippuu vaan vähän.
lines.text_kirja: Ei tarvitse, jos se tippuu vain vähän.
lines.gloss_en: No need, if it's only dripping a little.

judge.reason: Tarvii/tarvitse and vaan/vain are register variants; the negation and condition are unchanged.

puhe.text: Ei tarvii, jos se tippuu vaan vähän.

kirja.text: Ei tarvitse, jos se tippuu vain vähän.

judge.reason: Okei and selvä both mean 'OK'; mä oon is the spoken form of minä olen.
Nähään is the spoken form of nähdään; kohta and pian both mean 'soon'.

forms.why_en: Moi is the everyday spoken hello. Books and formal texts write hei.
The genitive singular adds -n for 'of': keittiö becomes keittiön.
The genitive singular goes before alla 'under': tiskiallas becomes tiskialtaan.
Alla means under and comes after its word: sen alla.
The form of olla, to be, for he, she or it. People say it the same way.
The partitive singular is used for some water: vesi becomes vettä, the si turning to tt.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Ei on its own answers 'no'. People say it the same way.
Paljon with the question ending -ko asks 'how much?'. Speech uses -ks: paljonks.
The partitive of se after en löydä: en löydä sitä.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.

Tippua 'to drip' doubles its last vowel for 'it': tippuu. People say it the same way.
Adds -sta for 'from': putki becomes putkesta, the i turning to e. Speech drops the last a.
This is how you tell someone to put: laita. It comes from laittaa, with one t.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Alle means 'to under, under it'. People say it the same way.
Speech shortens minä to mä. Books write minä.
Adds -en for 'I': tulla becomes tulen. Speech says tuun.
The genitive singular goes before päästä 'after': tunti becomes tunnin.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Kiitti is the everyday spoken thanks. Books write kiitos.

forms.lemma_meaning_en: to have to, to like, to hold
forms.why_en: Pitää, to have to, with the question ending -ko: pitääkö? Speech uses -ks: pitääks.
Minä with -n: minun pitää means I have to. Speech shortens it to mun.
Speech turns the ea at the end into ee: sulkea becomes sulkee. Books write sulkea.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
After ei the verb drops its ending: tarvita becomes tarvitse. Speech says ei tarvii.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Speech says vaan. Books write vain.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Okei is the everyday spoken OK. Books write selvä, which means clear.
Speech drops the l and stretches the vowel: olen becomes oon. Books write olen. From olla, to be.
Koti with -na means 'at home': kotona. The i of koti turns into o before the ending. You hear it every day.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
The passive form means 'let's see each other'. Speech drops the d: nähään.
Speech often says kohta 'in a moment' instead of pian.
